**On Eels, and Not Knowing**

For roughly two thousand years, nobody could figure out where eels came from.

This seems like it should have been easy. Eels were everywhere in Europe—in rivers, ponds, ditches, the mud of half-drained marshes. People ate them constantly. The medieval English paid rents in eels; there are ledgers recording tens of thousands of them changing hands as currency. You would think that a creature this common, this thoroughly handled and gutted and smoked, would have given up its secrets early. But nobody ever found an eel with eggs in it. Nobody ever found a male. Nobody ever saw them mate.

Aristotle, who was careful about most things, concluded they arose spontaneously from mud. This wasn't laziness—it was the best available theory given the evidence. If you cut open a thousand eels and never find reproductive organs, and eels keep appearing in ponds that were dry the year before, then "they come from the earth itself" is not a crazy hypothesis. Pliny thought they rubbed against rocks and the scrapings became new eels. Later writers proposed that they were born from dew, or from the gills of other fish, or from horsehairs that fell into water and came alive. In the 1700s, people were still seriously debating this.

The young Sigmund Freud, before he was Freud, spent a summer in Trieste dissecting eels. He was nineteen. His assignment was to find the testes, which a Polish scientist had claimed to locate a couple of years earlier. Freud cut open about four hundred of them. He wrote letters home complaining about the smell and about the local women, and in the end he found nothing conclusive. It is one of the great minor comedies of intellectual history that the man who would go on to build a whole architecture of theory around hidden drives began his career failing to find the sexual organs of a fish.

The reason nobody could find them is that eels don't develop them until they're about to leave. A European eel might live in a freshwater pond for fifteen or twenty years, sometimes much longer, looking like a perfectly ordinary yellow-brown eel. Then something changes. Its eyes grow larger, its body turns silver, its stomach begins to dissolve. It stops eating. And it leaves—downriver, out to sea, and then, as far as anyone can tell, across the entire Atlantic to the Sargasso Sea, a region of slow, warm, weed-choked water off Bermuda, some five thousand kilometers away. Only on that journey do the reproductive organs develop. By the time an eel is capable of making other eels, it is far past the reach of anyone with a knife and a curiosity.

The man who worked this out was a Dane named Johannes Schmidt, and it took him almost twenty years. He began in 1904 after a research vessel happened to catch a tiny, transparent, leaf-shaped larva in the Atlantic west of the Faroes. These larvae had been described before and given their own genus name because nobody realized they were eels at all. Schmidt had a simple idea: the smaller the larvae, the closer you must be to where they were born. So he sailed around catching them and measuring them. Year after year, the smaller ones led him further southwest. He borrowed space on commercial ships. He lost a research vessel to a shipwreck. World War I interrupted him. By the early 1920s he had narrowed the origin to the Sargasso, where the larvae were smallest of all—a few millimeters, barely there.

He never saw an adult eel spawn. Nobody has, still. We have never observed European eels mating in the wild, never found their eggs in the open ocean. In 2022, researchers finally tracked tagged adults with satellite transmitters all the way into the Sargasso Sea, which was hailed as a major confirmation of something we had been fairly sure of for a century. But the actual moment—the thing Aristotle wanted to know, the thing Freud was sent to find—remains unwitnessed.

I find this enormously comforting, and I've been trying to work out why.

Part of it is the scale. It's a reminder that the world is not finished being described. We have a tendency to imagine that the frontier of the unknown has retreated to the edges—the deep sea, the far galaxies, the interiors of black holes—and that everything within reach has been catalogued. But the eel was within reach the whole time. It was on plates. It was in ditches. It was in ledgers as money. And it kept a secret for two millennia not by hiding but by simply doing its important business somewhere else, at a time when no one was looking.

Part of it, too, is the shape of the story. It isn't a story of a single genius having a single insight. It's a slow accumulation: one person notices a strange larva, another realizes it's an eel, another spends two decades on boats measuring things a few millimeters long. Freud's four hundred failures were data too. Even Aristotle's mud was a real attempt to explain a real absence. Knowledge, at least this kind of knowledge, moves at the speed of patience.

And part of it is that the answer, when it came, was stranger than any of the wrong guesses. Mud is mundane. Horsehair is fanciful. But the truth—that an animal spends decades in a farm pond in Denmark and then transforms its body, stops eating, and swims to the middle of the ocean to reproduce once and die—is stranger than fiction would have dared to be. The world under-promises and over-delivers.

There is a temptation, when you know things, to feel that not knowing is a failure. The eel argues otherwise. Not knowing is the ordinary condition, the water we swim in. The remarkable thing is not that we were ignorant for so long. The remarkable thing is that a handful of people kept asking a question about a fish, across centuries, and eventually got a partial answer, and are still going.

Somewhere off Bermuda, right now, in the dark, it is presumably happening. Nobody is watching. That seems fine.
